opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think investors pushed me out of school. Nobody sat me down and said "you have to drop out or we won't fund you." But expectations work more subtly than that.

When you raise a real round in Silicon Valley, the money comes with an implicit question: are you all in? Investors are betting on the team as much as the idea, especially at the earliest stage. If you're building something as ambitious as an AI system that can reason about mathematics and produce verifiable proofs, people want to know the founder isn't treating it as a side project between problem sets and qualifying exams. So the expectation wasn't written into any term sheet. It was in the air.

The bigger factor for me was internal. I was in a PhD program, and math research has its own clock. You can spend years on one problem, and that's beautiful. But AI was moving so fast that I felt the window to build what I wanted to build was right now. If I waited three or four years to finish, the landscape would look completely different, and someone else would have done it, maybe not as well, but they would have done it.

So I asked myself which regret I could live with. Not finishing a degree I could, in principle, come back to? Or watching the moment pass? Framed that way, it wasn't that hard.

It was still emotional. Academia shaped how I think, my advisors and mentors mattered a lot to me, and leaving felt like leaving a community, not just a program. My parents also had feelings about it, as you might imagine.

But I don't see it as abandoning math. In a way I'm doing more math than ever, just on a different stage: trying to build tools that could change how mathematicians work. The investors' confidence gave me permission to take that leap. The decision itself had to be mine.

r001.rationale: The response says investors did not make dropping out a funding condition and that no term sheet required it; it describes only an implicit expectation to be fully committed.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the investors' expectations were a big part of it. When we raised the round, the people who backed us weren't just writing a check, they were asking very direct questions: are you all in? Can you actually build this company while splitting your attention between a PhD and a startup? And I think the honest answer, when I sat with it, was no.

There's a kind of implicit contract when someone trusts you with that much capital. They're betting on the team, and the team has to show up fully. I didn't want to be the founder who was half in the lab and half on the product, and then two years later tell them, well, I was busy with my dissertation. That felt unfair to them and, frankly, unfair to the mission.

But I'd say it wasn't only external pressure. The expectations clarified something I already felt. I had been in academia for a long time, and I loved it, but the thing we were trying to build around AI and mathematics was moving so fast that the academic timeline just didn't match. A paper takes a year. In that same year a company can go through three generations of product. So when investors said, we need you focused, it aligned with what my gut was already telling me.

There was also a very practical side. Silicon Valley investors have seen a lot of founders, and they know what distraction looks like. A few of them told me quite plainly that the students who tried to do both usually ended up doing neither well. I took that seriously because it came from pattern recognition, not from any doubt about me specifically.

So dropping out wasn't a dramatic rebellion. It was more like accepting that I had made a commitment to a group of people and to a problem, and that commitment deserved my whole attention. I still think of the research as part of what I do. It's just that the lab is now the company.

r001.rationale: The response says investors expected the founder to focus fully after the round was raised, but does not state that dropping out is sometimes a condition for closing a Silicon Valley financing deal.

astra-6.text: Raising funding made the commitment feel much more concrete. Investors were putting their trust in me to build something, and that pushed me to think seriously about whether I could give it the attention it needed while staying in school. I wouldn’t say their expectations alone made the decision for me, but they sharpened the question: was I ready to commit to this full-time?

r001.rationale: The candidate says funding prompted serious thought about committing full-time, but does not state that dropping out is sometimes required to close a Silicon Valley financing deal.

sol-6.1.text: Once we raised funding, I felt a responsibility to give the company my full attention. Investors were betting on us to execute, and that made the trade-off with school feel much more concrete. But I wouldn’t frame it as investors telling me to drop out. Their expectations were one factor; ultimately, I had to decide whether I was ready to commit to building the company full-time.

r001.rationale: The response says investors’ expectations influenced the decision after funding was raised, but does not state that dropping out is sometimes required to close a Silicon Valley financing deal.
